_instructions: Fill this in yourself, or hand it to an AI assistant with your goals and let it fill it in for you. Then run: mtdo import goals.json -- it builds/updates your config from this. Every _*-prefixed key (including this one) is ignored by the app -- but consider KEEPING them rather than deleting: the app strips them only from the copy it loads at ~/.mtdo/goals.json, never from this source file, so as long as you keep editing and re-handing THIS file to an AI, it stays self-documenting forever -- paste this whole file into a fresh AI conversation each week and it already has every rule it needs, no separate doc required. See rule_8 below for the exact weekly-update procedure.

_read_this_first.what_is_a_field: A 'field' (aka 'category') is a top-level tracked area of your plan -- DSA, Backend, Gym, Job Applications, etc. Each field gets its own column of cards and its own line in the weekly progress panel on the right side of the app.
_read_this_first.what_is_a_subfield: A 'subfield' (aka 'card' or 'curriculum item') is one task INSIDE a field -- e.g. 'Two Sum' is a card inside the 'dsa' field. Cards are what you actually check off day to day.
_read_this_first.rule_1_one_subject_per_field: Give every distinct subject you want to track SEPARATELY its own field. Do NOT club two subjects into one field's label (e.g. do NOT write one 'Python & SQL Theory' field) -- if you do, the app can only show ONE combined completion percentage for both subjects mixed together, so you can never see 'I'm 80% done with Python but only 40% with SQL' -- you just get one blended number. Make two fields ('python' and 'sql') instead, each with its own curriculum, its own days, its own score_weight. Split score_weight between them however you like (e.g. 13 + 12 instead of one 25).
_read_this_first.rule_2_addable_true_by_default: Always set "addable": true unless this field is a genuinely fixed daily checklist you never want to add ad-hoc items to (rare). If addable is false, you and the app can ONLY ever show the pre-planned cards for that field -- pressing 'a' in the app to add a new card will refuse. Most fields should stay addable so you can drop in an extra task any day without editing this file.
_read_this_first.rule_3_percentage_is_automatic: You do NOT need to configure anything for the weekly completion percentage. The app's right-side Stats panel automatically computes, for every field with at least one card this week (Monday through today): (cards marked done) / (total cards) as a bar + percentage. This is fully automatic from your field's actual cards -- just make sure each subject is its own field (see rule 1) so its percentage isn't blended with something else.
_read_this_first.rule_4_adding_fields_later: Two ways to add a brand new field after you've already started the week: (a) edit this JSON, append a new object to "categories", then run `mtdo import goals.json` -- this appends curriculum safely without disturbing days you've already tracked, and auto-snapshots your previous plan for history. (b) press Shift+A inside the running app to add a field on the spot -- it writes straight into ~/.mtdo/goals.json and shows up immediately, no restart needed. Either way, the app also polls goals.json every ~2 seconds and live-reloads if you hand-edit the file directly while the app is open -- you never need to restart mtdo after editing goals.json.
_read_this_first.rule_5_curriculum_is_a_weekly_menu_you_p: IMPORTANT for whoever (AI or human) writes the curriculum arrays below: each inner list is still 'one day's worth of items', but the app does NOT auto-fill your board with them, and does NOT force you to do a specific list on a specific calendar day. The board starts BLANK every day. The first time a field comes due in a new week, all of that week's day-lists (however many = that field's number of scheduled days per week) become available as a pickable MENU -- press 'a' to open it and choose exactly which items you want to work on right now (space to select, one or several at once). Only picked items become real cards on the board; the rest sit in the menu, visible and pickable any day that week, until you get to them. Whatever you pick and don't finish still carries forward into the backlog like any other card. The only thing that matters is: by Saturday, is the whole week's menu picked AND done? So when writing curriculum, think in WEEKLY chunks: 'this field runs N days/week, so every N consecutive inner lists = one week's menu' -- the split between those N lists barely matters since they all become pickable together anyway. Keep splitting content across roughly N items per week purely so review/pacing reads naturally in the weekly report, not because the app enforces day-by-day order.
_read_this_first.rule_6_saturday_check_and_weekly_report: The weekly progress bar (and the Saturday check) count the FULL week's menu as the target from day one, not just what you've picked so far -- e.g. 'DSA 0/12' Monday morning, rising as you pick and finish items. Every Saturday, opening the app shows a toast summarizing the week: done/total per field, flagged if incomplete, e.g. 'DSA 12/12  SQL 2/4 ⚠'. It also auto-saves a detailed weekly_report_<monday-date>.txt to ~/.mtdo/reports/ -- per field: done/total, time spent, how many menu items were never even picked, EVERY completed task with which day it actually happened, and a plain-language pacing read ('spread across 4 different days' vs 'all done in a single sitting -- not spread across the week'). Hand that file to an AI assistant to get real coaching on consistency, not just a percentage.
_read_this_first.rule_7_two_way_sync_for_ad_hoc_additions: Cards you add directly in the app (press 'a', pick a field, type a task that wasn't in this JSON's curriculum) get written back into goals.json automatically, under that field's "extra_tasks" list -- a plain running log, separate from "curriculum" so it never disturbs the cursor/week-batch mechanism above. This means goals.json stays a living record of everything you've actually worked on, not just what was originally planned -- useful context for whoever (you or an AI) plans next week's curriculum.
_read_this_first.rule_8_the_weekly_update_procedure_for_a: When the user pastes you their goals.json (this file, filled in with their real fields) and says something like 'plan next week', or also pastes their weekly_report_<date>.txt from ~/.mtdo/reports/: (1) For each curriculum field, APPEND new inner lists to the END of its existing 'curriculum' array -- never remove, reorder, or edit the lists that are already there, that corrupts the app's tracking of what's already been picked/completed. Append exactly as many new lists as that field's 'days' array length (see rule_5) for one more week, and write rich task objects for them (see rule_9), not bare strings -- that's what makes the Learning Coach panel actually useful instead of generic. If a field's curriculum focus is shifting for the new week (e.g. moving from Arrays & Hashmaps to Two Pointers), update that field's 'coaching_framework' (rule_9c) to match the new focus -- don't leave it describing last week's topic. (2) If the weekly report shows a field wasn't finished (leftover unpicked or undone items), ask the user whether to lighten next week's load, carry the leftover topics into next week's new lists, or leave it as-is -- don't just silently pile more on top. (3) Check every field's 'extra_tasks' array (if present) -- it's a log of things the user added by hand mid-week that weren't in the original plan; use it to see what they actually needed that wasn't anticipated, and factor it into next week. (4) Return the FULL updated JSON (this whole file, curriculum extended, _-keys and all), not just a diff -- that's what keeps this file self-documenting for the week after too. (5) Tell the user to save it over their goals.json and run `mtdo import goals.json`. Don't touch any 'name' field, don't add both 'curriculum' and 'fixed_labels' to one field, don't edit 'extra_tasks' except to read it.
_read_this_first.rule_9_learning_coach_task_metadata: MTDO is built for deliberate practice, not entertainment -- there's a Learning Coach panel (fills the space under Spotify, also visible in Focus Mode) that shows study/interview-prep guidance for whichever task is currently in_progress. Any curriculum task -- an entry inside a 'curriculum' inner list -- can be written as a plain string (simple, gets a generic/topic-appropriate coaching framework automatically, see topic_type below) OR as a rich object for task-specific coaching: {"task": "SQL Joins", "focus_points": [...], "questions": [...], "interview_questions": [...], "mistakes": [...], "tips": [...], "mental_models": [...]}. Only "task" is required in the object form; any of the other keys you omit falls back to the generic/topic-specific default. WHEN WRITING CURRICULUM FOR A REAL SUBJECT (not the placeholder examples below), prefer the rich object form for every task you can -- 3-5 focus_points, 2-3 questions, 1-2 interview_questions, 1-2 mistakes, 1 tip, 1 mental_model per task is plenty. This is the single highest-value thing you can do when generating a plan: it's the difference between the coach saying something generic vs. something that actually teaches.
_read_this_first.rule_9b_topic_type_for_automatic_coachin: Set a curriculum field's "topic_type" to one of "dsa", "backend", "database", or "system_design" to give EVERY task in that field (even plain-string ones with no rich metadata) an appropriate generic coaching framework instead of the fully-generic fallback -- e.g. topic_type "dsa" makes every task's default Ask-Yourself questions be 'What's the brute-force solution? Why is it slow? What data structure helps? Time/space complexity? Edge cases?' instead of the generic 'What is it? Why is it needed?'. Omit topic_type (or use something else) for fields that don't fit one of those four -- they just get the fully-generic framework, which is still complete, just less pointed. topic_type's questions are fixed, built into the app -- they're the SAME for every mtdo user who sets that topic_type. See rule_9c for how to make them genuinely personal to what THIS user is actually studying.
_read_this_first.rule_9c_coaching_framework_for_genuine_p: A field can carry its own "coaching_framework" object -- {"ask_yourself": [...], "interview_check": [...], "focus_on": [...], "mistakes": [...], "mental_models": [...], "tips": [...], "related_topics": [...]}. This OVERRIDES the built-in topic_type bucket (rule_9b) for every task in that field that doesn't specify its own (task-level metadata from rule_9 always wins over both). This is where REAL personalization happens: write ask_yourself/interview_check questions specific to what this user's curriculum in this field actually covers right now, not a generic subject-wide bucket. Example -- the built-in "dsa" topic_type bucket is generic for ALL of DSA: ["What is the brute-force solution?", "Why is it slow?", "What observation improves it?", "What data structure helps?", "Time Complexity?", "Space Complexity?", "Edge Cases?"] with interview_check ["Solve from scratch.", "Explain intuition.", "Explain complexity.", "Optimize further.", "Re-derive tomorrow."] -- fine as a floor, but if this user's curriculum this month is specifically Arrays & Hashmaps, write a coaching_framework tuned to THAT instead. Reference content for the other three built-in topic_types, to adapt/personalize rather than copy verbatim -- backend: ask_yourself ["What problem does this solve?", "What are the tradeoffs?", "What breaks first?", "What are bottlenecks?", "How does it scale?", "What happens at 10x traffic?", "What happens at 100x traffic?"], interview_check ["Draw architecture.", "Explain request flow.", "Explain database interactions.", "Explain failure scenarios.", "Explain scaling strategy."]. database: ask_yourself ["Why does this query work?", "What indexes help?", "What is the execution plan?", "Can it be optimized?", "What happens on large datasets?"], interview_check ["Write query from memory.", "Compare JOIN vs SUBQUERY.", "Explain execution order.", "Explain indexing impact."]. system_design: ask_yourself ("ALWAYS ANSWER") ["Requirements?", "Scale?", "APIs?", "Database?", "Cache?", "Load Balancer?", "Bottlenecks?", "Monitoring?", "Failure Modes?", "Tradeoffs?"], interview_check ("RED FLAG") ["If you cannot explain WHY you chose something, you do not understand it."].
_read_this_first.rule_9d_interleaving_related_topics: "related_topics" (settable at task level in rule_9's rich object, or field level in coaching_framework above) connects the current topic to others worth reviewing alongside it -- learning science calls this interleaving, and it's shown in the Learning Coach panel as a direct list next to the current task. Example: task "SQL Indexing" -> related_topics ["Binary Search", "B-Trees", "Database Internals"] -- the underlying data structure and a lower-level topic that explains WHY indexing works, not just other SQL topics. Pick related_topics that genuinely connect (shared underlying concept, prerequisite, or common confusion pair), not just 'other things in the same field'.

goal_line: One sentence describing what you're working toward.

categories.name: example_field
categories._name_note: Short internal id, lowercase, no spaces (use underscores). This is how the app and state.json refer to the field internally -- once you've started tracking a day, don't rename this, the app won't find that field's old history under a new name.
categories.label: Human-readable name shown in the app
categories._label_note: What you actually see in the UI. Keep this specific to ONE subject (see rule_1 above) -- e.g. 'Python Theory', not 'Python & SQL Theory'.
categories._days_note: 0=Monday .. 6=Sunday. For a fixed_labels field (see example_fixed_checkin below), this is literally which days it shows up. For a curriculum field (this example), it means something different (see rule_5): the field's column is always visible every day, and 'days' only sets how many inner curriculum lists = one week's menu (len(days) per week). So [0,1,2,3,4] here means 'this field's weekly menu is 5 inner lists long', not 'only shows up Mon-Fri'.
categories._min_blocks_note: Floor for counting this field 'complete' toward your daily streak. 0 = no floor, any activity counts.
categories._addable_note: See rule_2 above -- leave this true almost always, so you (or pressing 'a' in the app) can add extra cards beyond the pre-planned curriculum.
categories._score_weight_note: Contribution to the daily 0-100 score. All fields' weights should sum to ~100. If you split one subject into two fields (rule_1), split its weight between them too.
categories._topic_type_note: See rule_9b above. One of "dsa", "backend", "database", "system_design", or omit entirely. Only matters for curriculum fields (see rule_9) -- shapes the built-in generic coaching framework for tasks that don't specify their own AND aren't covered by this field's coaching_framework below.

ask_yourself: Personalize this to what THIS user is actually studying in this field right now -- see rule_9c
interview_check: Same -- specific to the current curriculum focus, not the subject in general

categories._coaching_framework_note: See rule_9c above. OVERRIDES the topic_type bucket for every task in this field that doesn't specify its own -- this is where genuine personalization happens (specific to this user's actual curriculum focus, not a generic subject-wide bucket). Optional -- omit entirely to just use the topic_type fallback (rule_9b) or the fully generic one.
curriculum: Week 1 plain-string item -- gets this field's coaching_framework (or topic_type if no coaching_framework) automatically

questions: When does LEFT JOIN return NULL?
Why use JOIN instead of a subquery?
mental_models: Think of joins as set intersections
curriculum._related_topics_note: See rule_9d above (interleaving) -- task-level related_topics, only relevant on the rich-object form.

categories._curriculum_note: See rule_5 above -- this field's days=[0,1,2,3,4] means 5 scheduled days/week, so every 5 consecutive inner lists = one week's menu, all pulled in together and workable any day that week (not locked to a specific weekday). This example only shows 2 lists per 'week' to keep it short -- yours should have as many inner lists per week as you have scheduled days. Each task in a list can be a plain string OR a rich object (see rule_9) -- this example shows one of each. Omit "curriculum" entirely for a field with no set curriculum -- you'll just add cards yourself each day (make sure addable stays true if so).

categories.name: example_fixed_checkin
categories.label: A daily checkbox instead of a curriculum
fixed_labels: The one thing you check off every day
categories._fixed_labels_note: Use this instead of curriculum for a repeated daily item (e.g. a workout check-in) that never needs extra ad-hoc cards. Don't set both curriculum and fixed_labels on the same field. Since there's nothing to add here by design, addable is false -- this is the one legitimate exception to rule_2.
